A design is a decision about **who you recruit and when you measure them**. That
one decision fixes which measures you are allowed to compute, and which biases
you have invited in.

## The four designs in one table

| Design | You start from | You then find out | Measure you get |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Cohort** | exposure | who develops disease | risk, rate, RR |
| **Case-control** | disease | who was exposed | OR only |
| **Cross-sectional** | neither; a snapshot | both at once | prevalence, POR |
| **Trial** | exposure you *assigned* | who develops disease | risk, rate, RR |

Read the "you start from" column carefully. It decides everything else.

## Cohort study

Take people **free of the disease**, record their exposure, follow them forward,
count who falls ill.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# 2,000 disease-free adults, exposure recorded at baseline, followed 5 years
cohort <- tibble(
  group   = c("Exposed", "Unexposed"),
  n       = c(1000, 1000),
  cases   = c(90, 30)
)

cohort |>
  mutate(risk = cases / n) |>
  mutate(rr   = risk / risk[group == "Unexposed"])
```

Risk 0.09 versus 0.03, so **RR = 3.0**.

Because you observed the whole denominator, you can compute a risk. That is the
cohort's defining privilege.

**Strengths.** You know exposure came first, so the time order is right. You can
measure several outcomes from one exposure. You get absolute risks, which is
what patients and planners actually need.

**Weaknesses.** Slow and expensive. Useless for rare diseases — following 2,000
people for a disease affecting 1 in 10,000 finds nothing. And people drop out,
which is a bias, not only a nuisance, if the ones who leave differ from the ones
who stay.

## Case-control study

Now run it backwards. Take people who **already have** the disease, take a
comparable group who do not, and look back at their exposure.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

# 200 cases of a rare cancer, 400 controls from the same source population
cc_study <- tibble(
  group    = c("Cases", "Controls"),
  n        = c(200, 400),
  exposed  = c(120, 120)
)

cc_study
```

```{webr}
a  <- 120   # exposed cases
b  <- 120   # exposed controls
cs <- 80    # unexposed cases     (200 - 120)
ct <- 280   # unexposed controls  (400 - 120)

# Odds of exposure in cases, versus in controls
odds_ratio <- (a / cs) / (b / ct)
round(odds_ratio, 2)
```

**OR = 3.5.**

::: {.callout-important}
## You cannot compute a risk here, and it is not a small point
You decided to recruit 200 cases and 400 controls. If you had recruited 800
controls instead, the "risk" would halve — while nothing about the disease
changed. Any risk or prevalence you compute from a case-control study is a
property of your recruitment plan, not of the world.

The odds ratio is the exception. It is unchanged by how many controls you
sampled, which is why this design works at all.
:::

**Strengths.** Fast, cheap, and the only practical design for a rare disease or
a long latent period. One cancer registry gives you cases it would take a cohort
twenty years to accumulate.

**Weaknesses.** Exposure is usually measured **after** the disease, by asking
people or reading old records. That opens two doors at once: people with a
disease remember their exposures differently (recall bias), and choosing the
wrong controls destroys the study (selection bias). Primer 9 is about both.

::: {.callout-note}
## Controls must come from the population that produced the cases
The test: if one of your controls had developed the disease, would they have
ended up in your case group? If yes, they are a valid control. If no — they live
in another district, or attend a hospital you did not sample from — they are
not.

Hospital controls are convenient and are the commonest way this design goes
wrong. People in hospital are ill, and their exposures resemble those of ill
people rather than those of the general population.
:::

## Cross-sectional study

One snapshot. Measure exposure and outcome at the same moment.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

survey <- tibble(
  obese     = c(TRUE, TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE),
  diabetes  = c(TRUE, TRUE, FALSE, TRUE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE, FALSE)
)

survey |>
  group_by(obese) |>
  summarise(n = n(), with_diabetes = sum(diabetes),
            prevalence = round(mean(diabetes), 3))
```

Prevalence **0.667 among the obese** and **0.2 among the rest**.

**Strengths.** Quick, cheap, and the right design for planning services. A
prevalence survey tells a district how many people need treatment now, which no
cohort will tell you.

**Weaknesses.** You cannot tell which came first. Did obesity cause the
diabetes, or did the treatment for diabetes cause weight gain? The design
contains no information that could answer that.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Prevalent cases are survivors
A cross-sectional study finds people who have the disease **and are still
around to be found**. Anyone who died quickly, recovered quickly, or moved away
is invisible.

So if an exposure makes a disease more fatal rather than more frequent, a
cross-sectional study can show *less* of that exposure among cases. The
association reverses. This is sometimes called incidence-prevalence bias, and it
is why these studies describe burden well and causes badly.
:::

## Randomised controlled trial

You **assign** the exposure, at random.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)

trial <- tibble(
  arm    = c("Intervention", "Control"),
  n      = c(500, 500),
  events = c(40, 70)
)

trial |>
  mutate(risk = events / n) |>
  mutate(rr   = risk / risk[arm == "Control"],
         rd   = risk - risk[arm == "Control"])
```

Risk 0.08 versus 0.14. **RR = 0.571**, **RD = −0.06**. About 17 people need
treating to prevent one event.

**Why randomisation is different in kind.** In every observational design you
can only adjust for confounders you thought of and measured. Randomisation
balances the confounders you never thought of, because the assignment is
independent of everything about the patient. No amount of adjustment does
that.

**Weaknesses.** Often unethical — you cannot randomise people to smoke.
Frequently impractical or unaffordable. And trial participants are volunteers
who meet strict criteria, so what works in the trial may not work in your
clinic.

## Choosing a design

Work through these in order:

1. **Is the disease rare?** Yes → case-control. A cohort will not find enough
   cases.
2. **Is the exposure rare?** Yes → cohort, sampled on exposure. A case-control
   study will not find enough exposed people.
3. **Can you ethically assign the exposure?** Yes, and you can afford it →
   trial.
4. **Do you need to know how common something is, right now?** →
   cross-sectional.
5. **Do you need the time order to be certain?** → cohort or trial. No other
   design gives it to you.

::: {.callout-note}
## A design is not "good" or "bad"
A cross-sectional survey is the wrong tool for causation and the right tool for
planning. A trial is the strongest design for efficacy and often a poor guide to
what happens in routine practice. The question is always *fit for this
question*, never *high or low in a hierarchy*.
:::

## Exercises

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: odds ratio from a case-control study"}
**Time:** 6 minutes

A case-control study of oesophageal cancer:

<table class="twobytwo">
<tr><th></th><th>Cases</th><th>Controls</th></tr>
<tr><th>Heavy alcohol use</th><td>96</td><td>109</td></tr>
<tr><th>Not heavy</th><td>104</td><td>691</td></tr>
</table>

Compute the odds ratio, rounded to 2 decimal places.

```{webr}
#| setup: true
#| exercise:
#|   - ex_or
#|   - ex_cannot
exp_case    <- 96
exp_control <- 109
une_case    <- 104
une_control <- 691
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_or
______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_or
#| solution: true
round((exp_case * une_control) / (exp_control * une_case), 2)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_or
#| check: true
# (96 * 691) / (109 * 104) = 66336 / 11336 = 5.852
if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 5.85))) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — OR 5.85. Heavy drinkers had almost six times the odds of oesophageal cancer. Because the disease is rare, this is also a fair guide to the risk ratio.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.17, tolerance = 1e-2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That is the reciprocal. The cross product puts exposed-cases and unexposed-controls on top.")
} else if (isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 0.47, tolerance = 1e-2))) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "That looks like 96/205: a risk computed from the exposed row. You cannot compute a risk in a case-control study, because you chose how many controls to recruit.")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right shape, wrong number. Multiply the two diagonal cells (exposed cases and unexposed controls), divide by the product of the other two.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "One number: (exp_case * une_control) / (exp_control * une_case), rounded to 2 places.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_or"}
Same cross product as Primer 7. The only difference is what the columns mean.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: what you may not compute"}
**Time:** 4 minutes

Using the same study, someone computes `exp_case / (exp_case + exp_control)`
and calls it "the risk of cancer in heavy drinkers".

What is that number, and why is it not a risk? Answer by assigning one of these
two strings to `answer`:

- `"a real risk"`
- `"an artefact of the sampling"`

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_cannot
answer <- ______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_cannot
#| solution: true
answer <- "an artefact of the sampling"
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_cannot
#| check: true
given <- if (is.character(.result) && length(.result) == 1) .result else ""
if (grepl("artefact", given, fixed = TRUE)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. Recruit twice as many controls and that number halves, while nothing about the disease changes. It measures your recruitment plan, not the world.")
} else if (grepl("real risk", given, fixed = TRUE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Not so. The denominator here is cases plus controls, and you chose how many controls to take. Double the controls and the number halves.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Assign one of the two strings, in quotation marks, to answer.")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_cannot"}
Ask yourself: if the investigators had recruited 1,600 controls instead of 800,
would that number change? Would the disease have changed?
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 3: pick the design (on paper)"}
**Time:** 5 minutes. No code.

Which design for each question?

1. Does a new antenatal counselling package reduce low birth weight?
2. Is a rare childhood liver cancer associated with a particular pesticide?
3. How many adults in this district have untreated hypertension?
4. Do night-shift nurses develop more metabolic syndrome over ten years?

::: {.callout-tip collapse="true" title="Answers"}
1. **Randomised trial.** You can ethically assign counselling, and you want to
   know whether it *works*, not only whether it correlates with something.
2. **Case-control.** The disease is rare, so a cohort would need an impossible
   number of children. Start from the cases.
3. **Cross-sectional survey.** "How many, now" is a prevalence question, and
   prevalence is exactly what this design gives you.
4. **Cohort.** The exposure (night shifts) is common and identifiable up front,
   the outcome develops over years, and you need the time order to be certain.

For 4, notice that a cross-sectional survey of current nurses would miss anyone
who left night shifts *because* their health deteriorated — the survivors are
the healthy ones. That is a real and well-documented effect, and a cohort avoids
it.
:::
:::

## What you should now be able to do

- Say what each design starts from, and therefore what it can measure.
- Explain why a case-control study yields an odds ratio and nothing else.
- Explain why a cross-sectional study cannot establish time order.
- Say what randomisation does that no amount of adjustment can.
- Choose a design from the question rather than from a hierarchy.
